analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments first this morning in 75-1301, Delaware Tribal Business Committee against Weeks and the related cases. Mr. Christensen, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. You will recall that this case poses the question of whether a three-judge federal court may hold unconstitutional a distribution statute passed by Congress distributing an Indian Claims Commission award, 10 percent to two federally recognized tribes, the balance to the members of the tribe per capita, thereby excluding. American citizens who have Delaware blood in them, but whose ancestors renounced the tribe and became solely United States citizens some 110 years ago. The court enjoined distribution of the fund under the statute to last until either Congress amended the statute or passed an entirely new one. The award was based upon a violation by the United States in 1856 and 1857 of an 1854 treaty, under which some of the lands then occupied by the Delawares and Kansas were to be sold at public sale with the proceeds held in trust by the United States for the benefit of the Delaware people. I'll get to that in the argument, but that it was for the Delaware people is extremely clear. As a matter of fact, they were sold at private sale. And in this case, it was found, or the Indian Claims Commission found, that the sale produced something in the neighborhood of a million point four million dollars less than a public sale would be. And that's the foundation of the award, which with interest today, I'm informed, amounts to some 13.7, 13.4 million dollars. After the 1854 treaty and the sale of the lands, in 1866, in the rush of white settlers into Kansas, the United States decided to remove the Delawares into Indian Territory. And it promised to sell their lands and then take the proceeds and buy them a place to live in Indian Territory. It had to make a deal with the Cherokees to get them in there because at that time, the United States was crowding more Indians into the Indian Territory and giving away or letting them occupy land with more Indians than there were land. But that treaty, and this is crucial to this case, of 1866, by which the Delawares were compelled to move into Indian Territory, contained an important exception. And that was, if a Delaware could prove that he'd adopted civilized ways, that he had supported himself for five years, he was given the option of renouncing the tribe and becoming solely an American citizen, and under those circumstances, he could stay in Kansas on land that already had been allotted to him or the equivalent of it. Some 21 adults chose to exercise that option in 1867. They, with their children, remained there in a few years. Their children also became American citizens. Now, that process was one of renunciation of the tribe completely, tribal affiliation, all interest in tribal funds, except they got a pro rata share as it then existed. And so they have been American citizens ever since. At that time, the Delaware tribe was actually in two branches. The main group was in Kansas. There was a smaller group that had wandered off down amongst the southern Indians that were expected to rejoin the main tribe, but they never did, and they're located in western Oklahoma. So you have today two federally recognized tribes before you, the Delaware tribe of Indians, which I have the honor to represent, and the absentee tribe of western Oklahoma. And where are your clients located? They're located in Oklahoma also, yes. In an area roughly in the Bartlesville area, and the others are the absentee tribes further west. Your group is called in the briefs the Cherokee Delawares. Correct. That's correct. Now, that name Cherokee, Your Honor, is a classification used by the plaintiff Weeks in this case. She set up classes and subclasses of Delawares, and she denominated my people Cherokee Delawares because they lived with the Cherokees, and they had certain rights as Cherokees. But the undisturbed finding of fact below is that they constantly had maintained tribal identity during this long span from 1867 or thereabouts to the time of the trial of this action. May I ask you one more question? I take it that your group or the group you represent came about separately after the 1854 treaty. Do I have my chronology right? No, not quite, Your Honor. The group I represent came about before Columbus landed here. They were the Delaware tribe of Indians that originally started out somewhere in New Jersey, and step by step, as you'll find it traced in the briefs and in the history, there's a long... No, I know that, even the last of the Mohicans tells us this. Yes. My question was directed at their going to Oklahoma and whether it was that journey that came after the 1854 treaty. Yes. That's the one. I misunderstood your question. I beg your pardon. It came after the 1866 treaty, didn't it? Yes. Yes. Yes. They moved, I think, in 1867. That's right. But it was after the 1866 treaty. Mr. Christensen, you said there were two groups in 1866. Was there not a third, the Muncees? Yes, but they are not part of this litigation. No, but they're relevant when we're trying to figure out what Congress was doing with the distribution of the guns. Well, yes, there were. The Muncees, as I understand it, had started with the tribe. They'd moved up into New York, and then they began to live with the Stock Bridges. I was born and raised in Oshkosh, Wisconsin. And right across Lake Winnebago from me were the Stock Bridges. Not until I got in this case did I discover they were really Delaware's. But the Muncees have been in Canada or Wisconsin for many, many years. Just how long, I can't tell you, Mr. Justice Stevens. Now, this brings us to the appellees, the so-called Kansas Delawares. Now, that, again, is a litigation classification. The Kansas Delawares are solely American citizens. There never has been a group of Indian citizens holding Indian citizenship known as the Kansas Delawares. Never in the past and not today. This is purely a litigation device. The ancestors of these people left the tribe in 1866 or 1867, exercising their options so to do. And they are no more... The 21 adults that you told us about earlier. Yes, sir. Yes, Mr. Justice Brennan. They are no more Delaware, political Delawares, than I am a political Dane because my grandfather left Denmark about the same time that they made this move and came over here and renounced Danish citizenship and took up American citizenship. Now, it's relatively easy, in my case, with a notion between us, to decide that I have no political rights as a Dane. But, of course, here we have these people of Delaware, some Delaware blood, who are living amongst all the rest of us and fairly near, in some instances, the political Delaware tribes, one of which I have the honor to represent. Do they live together in any recognizable group? No, no, they do not. They live all over the country. There's some 900 of them now? I understand a lot of them went out into California during the days of the Dust Bowl. They do not live together as a group. There is no group of Kansas-Delawares. It is just a classification put together as you would put a class of bondholders or of citizens in an ordinary class action case. But it is true, is it not, Mr. Christensen, that their ancestors, the 41 original Kansas-Delawares, are within the group that was wronged by the government's breach of the treaty? Uh, their ancestors were in the group when a wrong was done to the tribal property. To the tribal right. They were a member of the tribe at that time? Yes, yes. You're saying the Kansas-Delawares are kind of like a classification of American Danes? I beg your pardon? Are you saying that the Kansas-Delaware classification is kind of like a classification of American Danes? Correct. Correct. That's a question from someone with Swedish ancestry, I guess. Well, this brings me... My time is up, if it please the court. We stand for this case being non-justiciable. We think it's a better, cleaner way than going into this question of rationality. Thank you very much. All right, Mr. Christensen. Mr. Randall. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. Suppose this question were asked. Does the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment bar Congress from distributing tribal property only to the tribe and its members? We think, and I think the court will agree, the question seems to answer itself. Yet, in our view, that's the very question presented by this case. In fact, the question may be somewhat similar, as I'll expand upon later. The question may well be, does the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment prohibit Congress from giving tribal property to the tribe? I say tribal property because that is what we're dealing with here. That's what the more than $13 million that Mr. Christensen referred to, which is now gathering interest in the United States Treasury, represents. It's tribal property. No individual certainly has any vested rights in that property. This money was appropriated by Congress to satisfy a judgment of the Indian Claims Commission. The money was appropriated in 1969. That's when it became tribal property. The award of the Indian Claims Commission was to the absentee Delaware Tribe as plaintiffs and the Cherokee Delaware Tribe, or the Delaware Tribe of Indians, which is their more formal title. As representatives of the Delaware Tribe, the modern representatives of the Delaware Tribe, and the basis, as Mr. Christensen pointed out, is not a wrong that was done to an individual, Delaware, or a group of individual Delawares. The basis for the award was a wrong that was done to the Delaware Tribe more than 100 years ago when the United States breached its treaty commitment in 1854 and failed to sell the land at public auction and sold it instead at private sale. So we're dealing with tribal property. Now, what is Congress's duty when it has tribal property? Congress's duty is to determine what is the best use of that tribal property for the Delaware Indians. It's not only its duty, it's its power, its authority, its right. The 1854 Treaty, in fact, charged Congress with that responsibility for all money that was generated by the land sales. Now, Congress's judgment, that is, its judgment about how best this tribal property should be used, is reflected in the statute that the district court struck down in this case, statute that distributed money to the absentee Delaware Tribe and the Cherokee Delaware Tribe. Mr. Randolph, could I interrupt you? During the period between 1954 and 1966, during the period after the wrong was committed, 1854 and 1866, after the wrong was committed, but before the Kansas-Delawares became citizens, they were members of the tribe. Were they not? May I make one clarification? There's confusion, I think, perhaps, in this discussion and certainly in the opinion of the court. When we talk about Kansas-Delawares... Well, the Indians who are now known as Kansas-Delawares... Kansas-Delawares were not members of the tribe. Their ancestors were. Well, but... What would you like to call them? That's the name that's been given to them for purposes of this... The non-Delaware Indians. All right. The non-Delaware Indians were then Delaware Indians and members of the tribe. Yes. That's correct. And at that time, a wrong had been done to the tribe. Is that correct? Yes. And they had an intangible interest in the difference between what they actually got and what they should have gotten. They had, in effect, a cause of action, did they? Not as individuals. Certainly no. The tribe did, didn't it? The tribe had a claim, certainly. And when they elected to become citizens, did they not... were they not then entitled to prorate a share of the tribal assets? They were entitled, to use the precise terms of the treaty, to a prorate a share of the tribal assets then held in trust in the United States Treasury. In the United States Treasury or held in trust by the United States? By the United States. But do you think the claim arising out of the breach of the treaty was something the United States held in trust for these people? No. They held in trust for the Delaware tribe if there was anything that was held in trust. For the tribe while they were still members of it. Had the wrong been known... Let me put it this way. Had the wrong been known in 1866, would they have shared in the proceeds of the recovery? They, by they, you mean the ancestors of the people that... Yes, true. One never knows, first of all. I think that's rather speculative. Who knows what would have happened between 1857 when the money was realized in 1866. For all we know, the Secretary of the Interior could have decided that there was a good project since the Delaware Indians had so much money at that time. In which case, they would not have shared. I think that's somewhat speculative. There is a but-for relationship, I agree. But for the fact of the United States violation, it would appear that the ancestors of the plaintiffs in this case probably would have received more money. I agree. There's another but-for. You think it's just probably? Is there anything to indicate that they would have received less than their eloquent share of the tribal assets at the time they said? That would depend on what the tribal assets were. I'm saying they could have been depleted in the intervening years given the large sum that would have been in the Treasury at that time. But there's another but-for in this case. It's not just simply that. And I'll get to that. The other but-for is but-for the fact that they resigned from the tribe, they would be sharing in the tribe's assets today under the distribution statute. But let me continue. As I said, Congress's judgment about how best the tribal assets, which came into existence in 1969, could be used, is reflected in this statute. Well, did the tribal assets come into, wasn't there a tribal asset when they just had an intangible cause of action? Wasn't that a tribal asset? That was one, yes. So the tribal asset did not come into existence then at the time you said? The $9.7 million was nowhere to be found until 1969 when that appropriation is made. It's the tangible, that represents the present value of the cause of action, doesn't it? The present value of the cause of action held by the Delaware tribe. Correct. It was due, though. To the Delaware tribe. How long was that money due since the last hundred years? That's right. To the Delaware tribe. And this, which simply emphasizes my point, that this was tribal money. Well, when you say cause of action, Mr. Randolph, do you mean that the Delawares at the time of, that the 1866 or 1867, that the tribe could have sued the United States? No, they could not have sued. It took an enabling act of Congress. It took the Indian Claims Commission Act in order to allow them to sue 100 years later. So it really wasn't a shows in action. Well, it existed somewhere in space, I suppose, until Congress acted and I think it was that and nothing more. Well, it was a claim that could not have been asserted anywhere. Unless Congress... Except an appeal to the... Certainly. They could not have... They couldn't go to court back then. That's right. That's right. Because if they could have, they could have put a restrictive cover. Well, the question then is, the one thing I think that there's no dispute about is this is tribal money. And Congress has made a judgment about what should be done with it. If the judgment were in error, if the judgment reflected in that statute about what to do with the Delaware tribe's money, it was in error. Let me interrupt again because it's really quite important in my understanding of the case. The government had sovereign immunity before the procedure for asserting Indian claims was provided for. Does that mean, in your judgment, that there was no tribal asset simply because there was no remedy? I think, with all due respect, I think the question is irrelevant to the case. The fund that we're talking about came into existence in 1969. If you... I wish you'd answer the question, even though you think one can say there was a tribal asset in one sense and one sense only, that there was the possibility that sometime in the future, Congress might pass a law that would... That would remove... That would remove sovereign immunity and allow the tribe to bring a suit for something that was done to it a hundred years ago. But you would agree that the existence of sovereign immunity would not be inconsistent with the notion that there was a tribal claim. And that that's I think that tribal asset for a hundred years was worth about zero as far as what it was worth. I don't know what one would have paid in 1866 for that, but it would not have been very much in light of the history of... Well, the fair market value wouldn't have been very high, but it was an asset. Well... You do agree to that? In some sense of the word? In the sense that you're using it, yes. But I don't think that's important. The important thing is that the tribal... We're dealing with tribal property. And Congress has directed how the tribal property should be used. The tribal property, the Delaware tribe. If Congress' judgment was an error, if in fact that's a misuse of tribal property, one would expect a Delaware Indian to complain. You're misusing the tribal property. The Delaware tribe's representatives, the two tribes before the court. No Delaware Indian has registered such a complaint. No Delaware Indian tribe has registered such a complaint. The complaining parties, as Mr. Christensen pointed out, who designate themselves the Kansas Delawares, are not members of the Delaware tribe or the absentee Delaware tribe. So far as the complaint appears, they're not members of any Indian tribe. In fact, they're not a tribal entity at all. They're not an organized group. They are simply a class, and they are a class for one reason only, because of the federal rules of civil procedure. And they have but one thing in common. The one thing they have in common is simply this. They each have an ancestor who resigned from the Delaware tribe in 1866 and agreed never again to participate in the tribe's councils or share in its property. And that's the common thing that binds the class together. Now, in our view, it's difficult to understand how failing to give that Congress is failure to give. Individual, non-tribal, Delaware Indians, a portion of the Delaware tribal fund, means that Congress has properly, improperly decided how the tribal fund should be best used. The basis for going further in saying the Constitution was violated is, we think, all the more difficult to understand in view of the Court's repeated holdings over the years, that Congress has plenary authority to decide what should be done with tribal property, that the political branches of the government are charged with this responsibility, that the judiciary must defer to their judgment, and that is the court recently held in Morton v. Mankari, legislation dealing with Indians is constitutional if it fulfills Congress's special obligation to the Indians, and I stress that last phrase, to the Indians. In regard to the Kansas-Delawares, Congress has no special obligation to them as Indians, none whatsoever, and that point, I think, is not in dispute. Now, I think it's fair to say that appellies really do not meet our arguments on this score, and as a matter of fact, they don't even cite the Morton v. Mankari opinion in their brief. What they invite the court to do is follow a different path, a path that's marked out by decisions that do not deal with Indian tribes or Indians at all. Their argument is simply this, that it is absolutely irrational, there's no rational distinction between them and the Indian beneficiaries of the distribution statute. This means that the statute violates due process or more precisely the equal protection principles that are embodied in the due process clause. Now, by a rational distinction, I would suppose that one means a distinction that's not based on the flip of a coin or on whimsy, but on reasoning. If that is the test, and I think it is, then this statute certainly meets that test. Let me give the court the rational basis. It's quite simple. In distributing tribal funds resulting from a 1969 appropriation by Congress, the statute simply excludes those whose ancestors relinquished any interest in tribal property a century ago. That's the rational basis. At least that's one. Now, it's derived from Article 9 of the 1866 Treaty, which we were discussing a few moments ago. And that says that after the Apolle's ancestors resigned, they were not to share in tribal property. Moreover, the same provision, Article 9 of that same treaty, says that in addition to 80 acres in fee, which these ancestors would get, they're entitled to a prorated share of the tribe's funds, then held in trust by the United States. Then held in trust by the United States. The district court interpreted this provision to say that, well, it doesn't mean what it appears to mean. What it means is that the ancestors would be entitled to share in a future award. And the court said further, the reason we interpret it that way is because we have to interpret statutes in favor of the Indians. Well, we agree with the last proposition, but we think an interpretation in favor of the Indians is not in favor of the Dalawares, but in favor of the tribes that are before the court. I would like to say that the one point that the Delaware Indians constantly make, and make, I think, effectively through their brief, is the proposition that Mr. Justice Stevens alluded to. Simply this, but for the breach in 1854, my ancestor probably would have gotten more money when he left the tribe in 1867. Whether the individual Kansas Dalawares would have been benefited, one never knows. If my great-grandfather had more money in 1866, I don't know whether I would be better off today. But the fact is, the but-for relationship is the one point that the Kansas Dalawares pressed. If Congress had made a judgment to include them in the distribution on the basis of that reasoning, I think Congress would have acted rationally. I think that would have been within Congress' discretion. I also think, and the point I'm making to the court, is that it would likewise rational, derive from reasoning for Congress not to include them on the basis of another but-for reasoning. But-for the fact that your ancestors left the tribe, you would have been members of the Dalawares tribe and entitled to its tribal money, when it was appropriated in 1969. Mr. Randolph, your argument, of course, is based on the face of the statute, and you presume a rational basis for the Congressional decision. Do you disagree with their analysis of the legislative history that the real purpose of not including the catch-all phrase with this second distribution statute was to exclude the Munseys rather than the Kansas-Delawares? I wouldn't frame it that way. Certainly the Munseys were, I would put it in a class. The real purpose was to exclude a class of people who would share in the award because and only because their ancestors were members of the tribe in 1854. That, of course, included the Munseys. But the problems that Congress realized that applied to the Munseys applies, I think, applies well to the Kansas-Delawares. Let me explain. First of all, there's a question about how many Kansas-Delawares there really are. We don't know. This class has not been closed yet, as far as I'm aware. They say, and they say, let me just be sure if this is factually wrong and you straighten me out, they say that the problem with the third category with the earlier distribution pursuant with Claim 337 was that their Munseys were hard to identify and they were delaying the distribution one thing or another. But that the Kansas-Delawares, in fact, are an easily identifiable group and there isn't the same problem with respect to them. Is that incorrect? I'd like to respond. Yes. I think that's basically their argument. Let me respond to that. I'll have to use some citations. Take a look at, I would like, of course, to take a look at the appendix, page 9 of the appendix, the complaint of the Kansas-Delawares. Now, one would suppose that if the Kansas-Delawares were easily identifiable, that they would know how many Kansas-Delawares there are, at least be close to them. The complaint, paragraph 9, on page 9, states there are approximately 300 members of the subclass Kansas-Delawares. Now I'd like to refer the court to the opinion... Approximately 250 living members. Is that what you said? No. 300 members of the subclass Kansas-Delawares. of the subclass Kansas-Delawares. Now I'd like to refer the court to page, I think it's 38, of the opinion of the district court in the blue jurisdiction. this book. Page 38? Yes. Footnote 36. Page 38. I'm sorry, 39. Page 39, footnote 36. 39A. 39A. Footnote 36. By now, the number of Kansas-Delawares has risen from 300 to 678 that were reported to the court. Doubled. And now I'd like to refer the court back to the appendix that was filed to page 28 of the appendix. The very last two lines of page 28, which is a filing by the Kansas-Delawares, defining the class. Now the class has risen, or fallen, I don't know the chronology here, to approximately 1,000 members of the Delaware class. It's the last line on page 28 of the buff-colored appendix. More than... The evidence didn't back it up? I assume that this is the evidence the judge is talking about, not the complaint. The judge is talking about what has been reported to him by the Kansas-Delawares. And every allegation I am talking about is an allegation by the Kansas-Delawares. And they have 300, 678, 1,000. I don't think that the Kansas-Delawares are easily identifiable, because if they were, we would have known long ago how many Kansas-Delawares there were. I think the same kinds of problems, at least... I think the court can take that into account in crediting Congress's judgment. This is the same sort of thing that caused the problem with the Munseys, except the Munseys, there were 1,500 Munseys. Here, the allegation is there are at least 1,000 Kansas-Delawares. One never knows. In fact, I'd like to point out one further thing. I want to be sure I haven't lost the thread of your answer to my question. You say there is, in fact, difficulty in identifying the Kansas-Delawares. Absolutely. is there evidence in the legislative history that Congress was concerned about the problem of identifying Kansas-Delawares as opposed to identifying... No, and I think that proves my point. They're so difficult to identify, Congress didn't even know they existed. And they never made themselves known before Congress. They certainly didn't. They did share in the earlier award, didn't they? Yes. They shared in the earlier award. But there's no indication and no reference to this particular group singled out. They shared in the other award because there was a catch-all. So you would say there is no legislative history indicating a deliberate decision by Congress to exclude Kansas-Delawares? No, I think the legislative history is precisely that. Congress intended to, because Congress intended to include those and only those it specified. That has the effect of excluding the Kansas-Delawares and Congress so intended. As a matter of fact, that's the very reason they're suing in this case. And you say the rational basis is that there was another consideration for that. Yes. Well, I think there's a rational basis. There are a number of rational basis. One is the one I just mentioned, which is that the people that are excluded are people whose ancestors gave up any right to tribal property. As simple as that. There's another rational basis. Or a consideration. Or a consideration. Assuming one was needed. Yes. There's no allegation, I might add, that the 1866 treaty has been breached by Congress because they didn't pay a certain amount to the Kansas dollars. There's another rational basis, too. I mentioned earlier in the argument that the question here may be, in fact, whether the due process clause prevents Congress from distributing tribal property to the tribe. This statute is, in effect, in form, a distribution not to individuals directly. It's a distribution between two tribes. If one takes a look at the statute, which is set forth, it's 1294A, and it's set forth in a number of places, but since I've had the jurisdictional statement out, page 96A and 97A of the jurisdictional statement, one notices that the form of the award and the form of the apportionment is to the absentee Delaware tribe of western Oklahoma and to the and also to the Cherokee Delawares or the Delaware tribe as they're referred to. The fact of the matter is that after giving the money, this is the way the form of the award reads, after giving the money to the tribe, Congress directed how the tribe is to use 90% of that money, which is, of course, a normal function of Congress and the executive branch in regulating the affairs of a guard or an award, which a tribe technically is and still is. Mr. Randolph, Congress can conclude that members of the tribe are Indians, but if you're not a member of a tribe, what makes you an Indian? That's a very difficult question, Mr. Justice Marshall. One can take the definition, for example, in the Indian Reorganization Act, which defines what an Indian is for the purposes of that act. The Kansas dollars would not fit within it. You have to be a member of a recognized tribe, number one, or possess more than one-half Indian blood and be recognized as an Indian in the community in which you live. I don't think there's any evidence whatsoever that any of the people representing this class come within that definition of an Indian. There's common law definitions in some state cases, I understand, that say an Indian is a person who claims to be an Indian, who possesses a high degree of Indian blood, and who acts in the customary tribal ways and so on and so forth. For our purposes, I think the important question is not whether in some abstract sense the Kansas dollars are Indians, but whether in a federal context they are. And the answer to that is clearly no. They're not Indians because Congress owes no special obligation to them. They're not in any kind of trust status with the United States. There's no ward-guardian relationship between them. As a matter of fact, the question came up whether their councils contract there for representing them had to be approved by the Secretary of Interior. If they were Indians, it had to. The answer was no. It doesn't have to be. And they so argued, as a matter of fact, that it didn't have to be. Mr. Randolph, has Congress ever recognized in any official way the Kansas LOS since 1866? No. There is precedent. The question came up a question quite similar to this. in 1906 where there was another distribution to the Cherokee Delaware tribe. And in that distribution, the distribution was made to the Delaware tribe of Indians. The question came up, does that include the Kansas Delawares? In 1906, the answer that was decided upon by the Secretary of Interior and the Comptroller of the Currency, and we've got this set out in our brief, is no. The Kansas Delawares are people that are descended from those who renounced their tribal membership in 1866. and they're certainly not entitled to this portion of this award of $150,000, even though, I might add, that some of the wrongs that the $150,000 was to compensate for were wrongs that occurred prior to 1866. Mr. Randolph, can I ask one other question to be sure I have your position right? Assume arguendo, and I know you don't accept this, but that the ancestors of the Kansas Delawares were members of the class that was wronged by the United States when it breached the treaty in 1854. Assume further that the Indian Claims Commission intended the award to benefit all of the descendants of the class of all of the members who were wrong.
